name: Your Name
blurb: Makoto Shinkai's film about a city boy and a country girl who swap bodies
title: Your Name Explained: Plot Summary and Ending
description: Your Name explained: who Taki and Mitsuha are, the body swaps, the time gap and the comet, the ending explained, and the film's main themes.
h1: Your Name: Plot Summary, Characters and Ending Explained
answer: Your Name is a 2016 Japanese animated film written and directed by Makoto Shinkai and made by CoMix Wave Films. It opened in Japan on 26 August 2016 and runs 107 minutes; Shinkai also wrote a novel version published shortly before the film. Mitsuha Miyamizu, a high-school girl bored with life in the mountain town of Itomori, and Taki Tachibana, a high-school boy in Tokyo, start waking up in each other's bodies a few days a week. What begins as a comedy of swapped lives turns into a race against time as the two try to find each other.

head: Character
Who they are
rows: A Tokyo high-school student who works part-time in an Italian restaurant
A high-school girl in rural Itomori from a family of Shinto shrine keepers
Taki's older co-worker at the restaurant, whom he admires
Mitsuha's grandmother, keeper of the family shrine and its traditions
Mitsuha's estranged father, the mayor of Itomori
Katsuhiko Teshigawara and Sayaka Natori, Mitsuha's best friends

body: Beginning. Mitsuha is tired of small-town life, of her father's election campaigns and of the shrine rituals, in which she makes kuchikamizake, a sake made by chewing rice, as an offering. She wishes she could be a boy in Tokyo in her next life. Soon she and Taki begin waking up in each other's bodies. At first each thinks it is a vivid dream, but the odd reactions of friends and the notes left behind convince them it is real. They set rules for each other and keep diaries on their phones. As Taki, Mitsuha charms Miki Okudera and sets up a date for him; as Mitsuha, Taki makes her more popular at school. On one swap day Taki, in Mitsuha's body, goes with her grandmother and Yotsuha to leave the sake at the family's sacred site, a shrine in a crater on the mountain above town, and hears the grandmother talk about musubi, the threads that tie people and time together.

Middle. After Taki's date with Okudera, which goes badly because his mind is on Mitsuha, the swaps stop. Taki tries to call her and cannot get through. He draws the landscape of Itomori from memory and travels to the Hida region with Okudera and Tsukasa to find it. A restaurant owner recognises the sketch: Itomori was destroyed three years earlier, in October 2013, when a fragment of the comet Tiamat struck it during the autumn festival, killing hundreds of people, Mitsuha among them. The two had been living three years apart all along. Mitsuha's diary entries vanish from his phone, and his memories of her start to fade.

End. Taki climbs to the crater shrine and drinks the sake Mitsuha left there. He sees her life in a vision, including the day before the disaster, when she went to Tokyo to find him, found a younger Taki who did not know her, and gave him the braided cord he has worn on his wrist ever since. He wakes in Mitsuha's body on the morning of the festival. With Tessie and Sayaka he plans to evacuate the town: they knock out the power substation with explosives and use the emergency broadcast system. Taki goes to the mayor, who dismisses him. At twilight on the crater rim, Taki in 2016 and Mitsuha in 2013 meet face to face for a few moments. They agree to write their names on each other's hands, but Taki writes "I love you" instead, and before Mitsuha can write hers she is gone. She runs back to town, falls, sees the words, and goes to confront her father as the comet splits.

Taki wakes in his own time without remembering why he went to Itomori. History has changed: the comet still destroyed the town, but almost everyone survived, because the mayor had ordered an evacuation drill. Years later Taki, now job-hunting, and Mitsuha, who has moved to Tokyo, both feel they are looking for someone without knowing who. They see each other from passing trains, run through the city, and meet on a staircase by a shrine. They walk past each other, turn back, and both ask the same question: what is your name? The film ends there.

The literal mechanism is left loose. The swaps are tied to the Miyamizu family's shrine duties and to musubi, the grandmother's idea that time, like a braided cord, twists, tangles and joins again. The forgetting seems to be the price of changing the past: both lose each other's names, but a feeling remains, so the reunion is not chance but the threads pulling them back together. Some viewers ask whether the Mitsuha Taki meets remembers the swaps; the film does not say, and the open question at the end suggests they will start again as strangers.

Shinkai has said the film was partly inspired by a visit in 2011 to Yuriage, a coastal town wrecked by the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, where he felt it could have been his own town. Many Japanese critics read the film as a response to that disaster, imagining a world in which a town could be warned in time. Others take it more simply as a love story about connection across distance and time.

ul: Connection: musubi, the braided cord and the names written on hands all stand for bonds that survive distance and time.
Memory and loss: the two forget each other again and again, and the film asks what remains when a name is gone.
Disaster and survival: the comet's strike on Itomori echoes real disasters and imagines saving the people they took.
City and country: Mitsuha longs for Tokyo while Taki, through her, comes to love a mountain town he will later fight to save.
Tradition: the shrine rituals Mitsuha finds embarrassing turn out to be what makes rescuing the town possible.
Runtime: 107 minutes; original language Japanese, with an English dub.
Original story by Shinkai, who also wrote the novel version; the songs and score are by the band Radwimps.
Context: it is the first of three Shinkai films about disasters, followed by Weathering with You (2019) and Suzume (2022).
Content advisory: suitable for teenagers and most older children; there is some body-swap humour about touching, and the disaster scenes are not graphic.

check.q: What is the time gap between Taki and Mitsuha?
options: None, they live at the same time
check.why: Taki lives in 2016 and Mitsuha in 2013, three years before him.

options: A fragment of the comet Tiamat
check.why: A piece of the comet Tiamat strikes the town during its autumn festival.

check.q: What does Taki write on Mitsuha's hand at twilight?
check.why: They agree to write their names, but Taki writes I love you instead.

faq.q: Do Taki and Mitsuha remember each other at the end?
faq.a: Not clearly. Both have forgotten the details and each other's names, but each feels a strong pull towards someone missing, which is why they recognise each other on the trains and ask each other's names.

faq.q: How did the people of Itomori survive?
faq.a: In the changed timeline Mitsuha reached her father, and the town held an evacuation drill that moved residents to safety before the comet fragment struck, so almost everyone lived.

faq.q: Why did Taki and Mitsuha swap bodies?
faq.a: The film links the swaps to the Miyamizu shrine and to musubi, the grandmother's idea of threads that tie people and time. The connection is what lets Taki warn the town, but the film never explains it in more detail.
